To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
suicide and accidental death rates are increased among psychiatric patients.

the suicide rate among former psychiatric patients was 1.5 times higher than the suicide rate among the relevant control population, and the accidental death rate among former psychiatric was 1.3 times higher than that of the relevant control population.

suicide risk is increased for patients of both genders with acute schizophrenia, affective disorder, alcohol abuse, and drug abuse, and for male neurotic patients, and that accidental death risk is increased for men with personality disorder, for women with depressive disorders, and for patients of both sex aged from 30-49 years.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification, evaluation, and prevention of suicide among the general population and among high-risk groups.
the identification of high-risk groups of psychiatric patients who may be the focus of special efforts at prevention.
the development and testing of methods for the identification of psychiatric patients with an elevated risk of suicide or accidental death.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

psychiatric patients, especially those with schizophrenia, affective disorder, and alcohol and drug abuse, are at significantly increased risk for suicide and that those with personality disorders and those aged from 20 to 49 years are at significantly increased risks for accidental death.

risk for suicide is greater for women and for those with affective disorders and alcohol and other substance abuse; risk for accidental death is greater for those with personality and neurotic disorders and for those aged from the late twenties to the early fifties.

the risk of suicide is greater for men and women of most psychiatric diagnoses, and the risk of accidental death is greater for men with neurotic disorders and women with personality disorders.
Suicidal Behavior Among Psychiatric Inpatients in a General Hospital.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
psychiatric patients, especially those with schizophrenia, are at increased risk for suicide and accidental death.
the risk for suicide and for accidental death is greatest for patients who have been hospitalized for schizophrenia and affective disorders, for men, and for young people.
the risk for suicide is greatest among patients with schizophrenia and affective disorders; the risk for accidental death is highest among younger persons with personality disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk for suicide is not confined to any single diagnosis or to any particular subgroup of patients.
we need to be aware of the risk of suicide among psychiatric patients and take appropriate action to prevent it.

the risk of suicide is highest in the first year after discharge, and it is highest among those with schizophrenia, alcohol and other drug dependence, affective disorders (depression and bipolar disorder), and neuroses (depression, anxiety, phobias, etc.).
